strings.text: Welcome to The Wandering Inn! Mind giving that table a wipe?
Oh - hi! You've got a good face, you know that? Come in, sit down. I'll find you something warm - on the house, probably. Don't tell Lyonette I said that.
A young human, no armor, no weapon, no idea she is the strangest thing in this world. She moves like someone still deciding to be brave. The inn already leans toward her.
I am not queueing. I happen to be seated near where a queue would form.
I am not queueing. I happen to be seated near where a queue would form.
Off shift. Good chair, good fire. The wall can hold itself up for one night.
Nobody has found me yet. Do not be the one who does.
Nobody has found me yet. Do not be the one who does.
Off duty. I am told this is a thing a person can be.
Warm here. Two doors. I counted.
Evening, {addr}. No business tonight, you'll be glad to hear.
Sit down properly if you are going to sit.
The tables are covered. Nothing more to carry out until tomorrow.
You carry the laden tray out to the tables.
Mind the floors, they're just done.
Lyonette's chin lifts, then softens despite itself. You're kind. People are not, usually, to the help. ...It is a small thing. It is not nothing. Sit where you like; I'll bring something hot.
A human girl playing at composure a size too large for her. Her hands know trays; her chin knows courts. The two have not finished arguing.
The kettle wants yarrow before it gives anything back.
A kettle, singing low. It's just a kettle, unless you know otherwise.
[Hedge Remedy] — The inn's kettle does in a pinch, just like she said. The steam settles into something kinder.
The kettle's on. The inn won't mind one more thing brewing, so long as it means well.
A working counter, scrubbed and stocked. The kitchen has standards, and they're looking at you.
[Advanced Cooking] — Knife-work first, then the pan, then the part nobody can teach. The plate comes out arguing for seconds.
Good stock, better knives, and nobody using either. A real cook could turn this counter into a meal worth naming.
The good copper pan, hung out of easy reach. Erin's rule, probably.
[Signature Dish] — The pan remembers you now. What comes out of it isn't dinner, it's a reputation.
The good copper pan. It's been waiting for a dish that deserves it.
You don't know your way around a stew pot. Yet.
[Basic Cooking] — The stew comes out rich and hot.
The stew's at the turn. Someone who knows a pot could bring it home.
The order's a mess and you haven't the first idea how to stretch it. Not yet.
[Basic Cooking] — You thin the stock, fold in day-old bread, and stretch the short order into a full service. Lyonette's shortfall vanishes into the pot.
Three plates ordered, one pot of stock. You could stretch it to cover them all. Nothing leaves the kitchen in your hands.
A plain plank door, warped at the bottom from a hundred winters. Nothing about it looks like it goes anywhere but the pantry.
The frame and the old marks under its paint both want a trained eye — and maybe more than one kind.
[Detect Magic] — The old wardwork wakes just enough to be read: someone bound this cellar's door long before it learned to go elsewhere.

[Observe] — The grain of the frame isn't grain at all: a pattern worked into the wood, old and deliberate, repeating around the jamb like a held breath. It doesn't move while you watch it. It moves the instant you look away.
Onions, a sack of soft potatoes, a shelf of jarred somethings gone dusty. The pantry door, same as it's always been.
The find leans against the pantry frame, unhung, with the old plank door stacked out of the way behind the flour sacks. Pisces has not stopped circling it since the wagon. Ask him about it.
A moment. I am counting the ward's repeats, and you are extremely countable.

He has taken his coat off, which for Pisces is manual labour. One hand rests flat on the hauled door's face, the way a physician rests a hand on a patient, and he is listening to something no one else in the room can hear.
Something scratches behind the pantry wall, patient and small. Probably nothing. Probably.
The scratching has become a chewing. The Door strains for somewhere it cannot reach yet, and something on the way there has found the gap and has teeth.
The vines part like a curtain, and the light beyond doesn't flicker.
Plaster, old and thin, and a nail with nothing hung on it. If something is meant to be here, it isn't yet.
Bare wall. A nail with nothing hung on it.
A door of living vines, woven shut and breathing faintly of green. It wasn't here before, and it doesn't pretend otherwise.
[Basic Cleaning] — The table is spotless.
The table's a mess of rings and crumbs. It wants a proper wipe-down.
Ask me about the vault again and I'll start charging Pisces rent.
My arm's still fine.
I am still counting exits. There are still two.
Ask me about the vault again and I'll start charging Pisces rent.
My arm's still fine.
I am still counting exits. There are still two.
The inn's room register, open to today. Lyonette's handwriting could win awards; the prices underneath it could start fights.
Faded arcane script. You can't read a word of it. Whoever penned this knew magic you don't. Someone in the city must.

With what Pisces beat into you, the faded script stops being noise: it is a warding treatise, old and patient, and it keeps circling one subject. A door. Bound, sealed, and fed — somewhere close. He would want to see this.
[Light] — A steady white orb settles into the lantern's glass.
The wick's dry and ready. All it wants is a light that doesn't need a match.
Innkeeper! Anyone?
Off the clock, for once. Don't tell the Guild I remember how to sit down.
The market can keep until morning. A good bowl and a warm fire, yes?
One night off. I have already mapped every exit twice. It is a sickness.
The hall on the other side, and a bolt on this side. The bolt is most of what the lease bought.
Made up tight, corners squared. Lyonette did that, and she will know if you undo it badly.
Your own room, and a door you can shut behind you.
Your own room, and bedding aired for you rather than for whoever comes next.
Your own room, the best bedding in the house, and a shut door between you and all of Liscor.
Your own footlocker. Nothing in it yet that needs a key.
A plain footlocker at the head of the bed, hasp and no lock. Everything you own would rattle around in it.
The desk is yours to use. Nothing on it yet is asking to be done.
A narrow desk under the window, one drawer, and a pale ring where somebody set a cup down for a whole winter.
Nothing on the shelves yet. Give it a season.
Three shelves and you have filled none of them. Depending on the hour that is a sad thing or a hopeful one.
You hang the day's coat and it stays hung. It is a small thing and it is not nothing.
Pegs worn pale at the shoulder height of forty travellers who hung a coat here and went away again.
Nothing there — just your own four walls, and the particular quiet of a room nobody else is paying for.
The key turns like it has been waiting to. Your room, and nobody else's.
It doesn't budge.
Shut, and the card slot in the frame is empty. Somebody paid for this one once and stopped.
Your name in the card slot, in Lyonette's ruled hand, and the key for it somewhere in your pack.
It doesn't budge.
Your own bed.
Your own bed, and a mattress that no longer remembers the last guest.
Your own bed, thick blankets, and a shutter that actually closes.
Your own room, warm and quiet, with a bed you are almost sorry to leave.
Locked. Lyonette keeps exactly one door in this inn that isn't anyone's business but hers.

Lyonette's door, shut the way she shuts most things: completely, and without discussion. Whatever the room looks like behind it, you'll have to imagine it; she's not one to leave doors, or herself, half open.
